hook: J.C.R. Licklider trained as an experimental psychologist, earning his PhD at the University of Rochester before working on psychoacoustics at Harvard during the Second World War. He later moved into engineering circles at MIT, where hands-on exposure to early computers convinced him that machines could become active partners in human thought rather than passive calculators. In 1957 he ran a self study tracking his own workday and found that most of his time went to mechanical tasks that stood between him and actual thinking, an observation that fed directly into his influential 1960 paper Man-Computer Symbiosis, which argued that people and computers should work together in close, real time partnership. In 1962 he became the first director of the Information Processing Techniques Office at the Advanced Research Projects Agency, where he funded university computer science research across the country and, in an internal 1963 memo, sketched an early vision of computers linked together into what he called an intergalactic network. That funding program and the community of researchers it supported helped lay the intellectual groundwork that led to the ARPANET later in the decade.

quick_facts: Trained as an experimental psychologist, earning his PhD at the University of Rochester
Worked on psychoacoustics at Harvard's Psycho-Acoustic Laboratory during World War II
Published Man-Computer Symbiosis in 1960, arguing computers should be active partners in human thinking
Became the first director of ARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office in 1962
Sketched an early vision of a globally networked computing system in a 1963 internal memo

achievements.title: Man-Computer Symbiosis, 1960
achievements.impact: Argued that computers should function as active partners in real time human thinking rather than as passive calculating tools, an idea that reoriented decades of interactive computing research.

achievements.title: Director, ARPA Information Processing Techniques Office, 1962
achievements.impact: Used the office's funding to support university computer science research across the United States, building the research community that later produced the ARPANET.

achievements.title: Vision of a networked computing system
achievements.impact: In internal ARPA memos he described a future in which geographically separated computers and their users could interact as if part of one connected system, anticipating key features of computer networking.
